body_markdown:
*The Hagerty Price Guide Indexes—first published in 2009—are a series of stock market-style indexes that average the condition #2 (“excellent”) values of representative vehicles, or “component” cars, from a particular segment. These indexes are updated quarterly and provide an overview of how these segments of the collector car market are performing overall, as well as relative to each other.*


The summer auction blitz is over with the headlining[Monterey auctions](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/2026-monterey-car-week-auctions-shatter-record-with-756m-in-sales/) in the rearview and plenty of market activity to discuss from them. Most obvious was the supercar/hypercar market picking up pace like a runaway train, with sales records smashed left and right. Coming back down to earth, more mainstream collectible markets were a mixed bag.


Of the 11 indexes we track, six posted a gain ([British Cars](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-british-car-index) ,[Postwar German](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-german-car-index) ,[Affordable](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-affordable-classics-index) ,[RADindex](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-radindex) ,[Trucks and SUVs](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-truck-and-suv-index) ,[Supercars](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-supercar-index) ), two lost ground ([Ferrari](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-ferrari-index) ,[1950s American](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-1950s-american-car-index) ), and three remained steady ([Blue Chip](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-blue-chip-index) ,[American Muscle](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-american-muscle-car-index) ,[Japanese](https://www.hagerty.com/#h-japanese-vehicle-index) ). Like the previous period, the overall market remains mixed but a trend is emerging. More modern vehicles are doing well, while traditional classics are not a guaranteed win. For example, several older cars in the German Car Index gained drastically, but the 1950s American Car Index took a small step back. While the market is starting to come into focus, some segments may take longer to find their footing.


## Blue Chip Index


Broad Arrow


*The Hagerty “Blue Chip” Index of the automotive A-List is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 25 of the most sought-after collectible automobiles of the post-war era.*


October marks the second straight quarter for Hagerty’s Blue Chip Index tracking no meaningful movement. While the overall number didn’t move, there was plenty of action with the component cars. With 25 cars tracked, seven gained in value while five lost enough to offset those increases.


Percentage movement was restrained among those that did see change. Only one—the 427cid/435hp 1967 Corvette—moved more than 5%. Despite all the attention paid to Monterey and the top of the market in recent months, the auctions in August did little to move the needle for the older, more established top shelf cars in this index. As we head into fall and winter, few opportunities to check in on the top of the market come up, which means blue chip collectors are poised to hold position through the end of the year.


## British Car Index


Paul Stenquist


*The Hagerty Index of British Cars is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 10 of the most iconic British sports cars from the 1950s-70s.*


After last quarter’s 2% increase, Hagerty’s British Car Index showed more positive movement by increasing by another 1% over the past three months. While cars like the Austin-Healey 3000 Mk III and Series I Jaguar E-Type lost 2% and 5%, respectively, the big news came in the form of a 15% increase for the Triumph TR6 and MGA 1600. Smaller increases came in for the Mk II Sunbeam Tiger (6%) and Austin-Healey 100M Le Mans (3%).


We are looking at the British Car Index with cautious optimism. Recent increases are encouraging, but they come after years of downward movement, and it’s unclear how big the recovery here will be or how long it will last.


## Ferrari Index


Ferrari


*The Hagerty Ferrari Index is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 13 of the most sought-after street Ferraris of the 1950s-70s.*


Following a huge 9% increase last quarter, Hagerty’s Ferrari Index settled back down, tracing a 1% loss. The previous term’s jump had everything to do with the 250 LM experiencing a sizable nudge upward, while this term is more of a return to reality.


Of the 13 component cars, six fell in value, most notably the 250 GT SWB (-8%), 250 GT PF (-4%) and 250 GT Lusso (-6%). The sole increase was the 330 GTC, which gained 5%. This all comes on the heels of August’s Monterey sales, which are traditionally the main auction event for Enzo-era Ferraris. This year, they were overshadowed by their modern counterparts both in number of cars offered and in buyer enthusiasm. Classic Ferraris will always be relevant, and at the moment they’re relatively stable.


## American Muscle Car Index


Mecum


*The Hagerty Index of American Muscle Cars is a stock market-style index that averages the values of the rarest and most sought-after muscle cars.*


After last quarter’s 2% rise, Hagerty’s American Muscle Car Index remained steady heading into autumn. The previous increase was largely influenced by one car, the AMC AMX SS. Following that one-off, the index settled back into a regular pace.


While there was no major change to the index overall, there was some activity under the hood. Of the 15 component cars, six tracked some movement. Two gained ground: the 1970 Buick GS 455 (4%) and the 1969 Mustang Boss 429 (19%), which had multiple strong showings over the summer. Offsetting these were decreases for the 1968 Murcury Cougar GT-E (-10%) 1970 Oldsmobile 4-4-2 W30 (-6%), Plymouth Hemi Superbird (-4%), and 1964 Impala SS 409 (-2%). Unseen beyond this index, many rank and file muscle cars have been experiencing a gradual softening in value, suggesting an emerging trend for the segment.


## German Car Index


Sean Smith


*The Hagerty Index of German Cars is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 21 of the most sought-after cars from BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Porsche from the 1950s-70s.*


Hagerty’s German Car Index tracked a surprising 7% increase following a long string of gradual ups and downs. Ten component cars of the 21 total gained value. Just one, the Mercedes-Benz 280SL, lost value with a 6% drop.


Most of the increases were in the Porsche 356 family, chiefly the Pre-A Gmünd cars gaining 33% after a very early, very special 356 (non-Gmünd) traded for a staggering $2.2M this past quarter, hinting at what enthusiasts would be willing to pay for even earlier models. But growth happened in other areas of the traditionally sleepy 356 segment with the 1959 356A Super Coupe (3%), 356B S90 Roadster (6%), and 356C 1600 SC Coupe (7%) all tracking upward after a long period of stagnation. Increases for the Mercedes 190SL (15%) and Mercedes 600 (13%) helped push the index up further.


While the Monterey auctions may not have been helpful to the classic Ferrari market, the classic Germans flourished, though this level of increase may be a blip we won’t see again for some time.


## 1950s American Car Index


Mecum


*The Hagerty Index of 1950s American Classics is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 19 of the most sought-after collectible American automobiles of the 1950s.*


Hagerty’s 1950s American Car Index reversed last quarter’s 1% gain with a 1% loss, returning to its slow, downward trajectory. Just six of the 19 component cars showed movement, with most of those movers shedding value.


On the upswing were the 1958 Chevrolet Impala Convertible (7%) and 1953 Oldsmobile 98 Fiesta (8%), while the remaining four movers lost ground. These were the 1957 Ford Thunderbird (-15%), 1956 Ford Fairlane Sunliner (-12%), 1957 Ford Fairlane Skyliner (-12%), and 1955 Packard Caribbean (-10%).


As the collector car hobby trends younger and as newer collector cars become the focus, 1950s American cars have experienced a gradual softening as their core enthusiast base ages. But shrinking values aren’t necessarily a bad thing. These cars are pure Americana and as the segment becomes more affordable, it opens up the doors to new, budget conscious enthusiasts to step in and carry the torch.


## Affordable Classics Index


Hagerty


*The Hagerty Index of Affordable Classics is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 13 undervalued cars, priced around $40,000, from the 1950s-70s.*


Following a 3% increase, Hagerty’s Affordable Classics Index tracked its largest gain since 2024. Of the 13 component cars representing this traditionally active area of the hobby, four showed movement. All four were increases.


The biggest gains were for the 1970 Chevrolet Camaro SS (12%) and Volkswagen Karmann Ghia (11%), with additional help from the 1965 Ford Mustang GT (4%) and 1969 AMC Javelin (1%). These bright spots represent areas where “average” collector cars are still thriving despite a shift to newer models by the wider collecting audience. It’s a good sign for the countless enthusiasts still enjoying these cars.


## RADindex


Volkswagen


*The Hagerty RADindex is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 21 collectible vehicles from the 1980s and 1990s.*


Hagerty’s RADindex posted its largest gain in four years, rising by 6% over the last quarter. The market for the 21 component cars was an extremely active one as well, with 13 of them tracking movement.


An impressive nine vehicles gained value, led by the 1987 Buick GNX (30%), Mk II Volkswagen Golf GTI (24%), and Ferrari Testarossa (14%). These gains and others were tempered by just four cars losing value, with the biggest loss attributed to the C4 Corvette ZR-1 (-12%), followed by the Z32-series Nissan 300ZX (-8%), FD Mazda RX-7 (-4%) and Porsche 944 (-2%).


RAD era cars have been steadily gaining in as the hobby Gen Xers and millennials become the primary drivers of the collector car market. Cars from the ’80s and ’90s are relatable to these generations and carry immense nostalgia, driving collecting habits. The recent spike to the index further demonstrates the staying power of these cars.


## Truck and SUV Index


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


*The Hagerty Truck and SUV Index is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 19 collectible trucks and SUVs from the 1940s to the 1990s.*


Hagerty’s Truck Index posted a modest 1% increase in the past quarter after showing no movement over the previous one. The activity behind the increase shows a more nuanced market for trucks.


There were six gainers and five losers out of the 19 component trucks, with the biggest increases coming on the newer side of the market with FJ60 Toyota Land Cruisers (10%), 1980s Toyota Pickups (7%) and Jeep Grand Wagoneers (8%). Meanwhile, losses came for long-established vehicles like Chevrolet Series 3100 pickups (-10%), first gen Broncos (-6%), and FJ40 Land Cruisers (-5%).


These changes continues the trend from last quarter where the market is showing discernment and restraint amongst historically expensive trucks and enthusiasm amongst newer, more readily drivable ones.


## Japanese Vehicle Index


James Lipman


*The Hagerty Japanese Vehicle Index is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 19 collectible Japanese vehicles from the 1960s to the 2010s.*


Following the previous quarter’s 11% jump, Hagerty’s Japanese Index understandably needed to catch its breath, and it tracked no serious movement for this recent update.


A quick peek under the hood does reveal mixed signals, though. Ten of the 19 component cars showed movement, with an even split of ups and downs. Gains included mass-produced models like the NA Mazda Miata (7%), 80s Toyota Pickup (7%), and DC2 Acura Integra (6%) lending a hand. Meanwhile, losses by some of the segment’s most recognizable models like the R32 GT-R (-7%), Nissan 350Z (-15%), and FJ40 Toyota Land Cruiser (-5%) offset those gains. Like with Trucks, the Japanese segment is one that appears to be maturing as buyers show more discernment and less willingness to spend wildly just to secure a car. This is a good sign for the segment’s longevity.


## Supercar Index


Broad Arrow Auctions


*The Hagerty Supercar Index is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 15 collectible modern supercars and hypercars.*


Hagerty’s Supercar Index is not slowing down, and rose by 14% over the last quarter. In the past 12 months, supercars and hypercars have been the best performing market segment, with the index rising a staggering 45% over the time period. Twelve of the 15 component cars showed growth, with the remaining three remaining static.


Most of the increases were in double digit percentage increases on cars that are already incredibly expensive. From the Ferrari F50 (20%) to the McLaren F1 (25%) and the 2005–06 Ford GT (18%), the supercar segment remains white hot with no signs of abating.


Just when it seems like this corner of the market has peaked, it continues to grow. It is of little relevance to the average enthusiast, but for those with the means looking to get into supercars, it’s important to approach with caution. Continued growth such as this is never guaranteed.
